blogs.title: New research: Virtual machines remain central to cloud native infrastructure as AI workloads evolve
blogs.content: Posted on November 9, 2026 by Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Broadcom A Linux Foundation Research study, sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, explores how organizations are using virtual machines alongside containers, and the growing importance of workload isolation for AI. Cloud native infrastructure continues to evolve as organizations support an increasingly diverse mix of applications and workloads. While containers and Kubernetes have become important parts of modern infrastructure, virtual machines (VMs) continue to play a significant role in production environments. New research from Linux Foundation Research, sponsored by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) and Broadcom, provides insight into how organizations are using VMs today, how they expect their infrastructure to evolve, and the role of virtualization in supporting emerging AI and agentic workloads. The report, Virtual Machines, Agentic AI and the Mix of Workloads: Findings from the 2026 Cloud Native Workloads Survey , draws on responses from 492 cloud native practitioners and leaders surveyed in September 2026. The findings highlight an important characteristic of today’s infrastructure: organizations are operating a mix of workload types, with VMs and containers frequently forming part of the same broader infrastructure strategy. Virtual machines remain a significant part of production infrastructure One of the report’s central findings is the continued prevalence of virtual machines. Across respondents, VMs accounted for an average of 53% of production applications , with 51% reporting that at least half of their production applications run as VMs. The research also suggests that this is unlikely to change dramatically in the near term. Among respondents who answered both the current and future workload-share questions, 71% expect the proportion of their production applications running as VMs to remain within the same range over the next 12 months. Organization size also plays a role. Respondents from organizations with 10,000 or more employees reported an average VM share of 64%, compared with 45% among organizations with fewer than 500 employees. These findings demonstrate the continued importance of understanding and supporting diverse workload requirements. Rather than indicating that one deployment model is replacing another, the research describes an infrastructure landscape in which multiple approaches coexist. VM and container teams are increasingly working together The research also examines how organizations manage their VM and container environments. 61% of respondents described their VM and container administration teams as collaborative or fully integrated , while 14% reported that the teams operate independently in silos. This coordination is relevant to the cloud native community as organizations consider how to manage different workload types while maintaining consistent operational practices. The report also identifies adoption of Kubernetes-based VM management. Among respondents running VMs, 8% reported using KubeVirt to manage virtual machines on Kubernetes. KubeVirt, a CNCF project, extends Kubernetes to support VMs as Kubernetes-managed resources, enabling organizations to manage virtualized and containerized workloads through Kubernetes. The research does not establish how all organizations technically combine their VM and container environments. However, it provides evidence that coordination between the teams responsible for these workloads is already common. AI and agentic workloads are contributing to demand for virtualization As organizations explore AI and agentic applications, workload isolation is becoming an important infrastructure consideration. AI agents may generate and execute code, interact with external tools, and access data or systems on behalf of users. These capabilities introduce security considerations, particularly when organizations need to contain potentially unpredictable code execution. The survey found that 34% of respondents expanding their VM footprint cited AI and agentic workloads as a contributing factor . Security and isolation requirements were also cited by 47% of respondents expanding their VM footprint, alongside improved hardware resource utilization (48%) and growth in VM-based applications (53%). The report explores several approaches organizations use to isolate AI workloads, including hardware-level VM isolation, containers running within VMs, and MicroVM sandboxing. Among respondents providing valid answers, 62% reported using at least one of these VM-based isolation approaches at the time of the survey. Looking ahead, respondents indicated growing interest in additional isolation measures: MicroVM sandboxing: 20% reported current use, compared with 30% planning to use it in the next year. Confidential computing: 12% reported current use, compared with 26% planning to use it in the next year. Containers within VMs: 40% reported current use, with 41% planning to use this approach. These are reported plans rather than confirmed future deployments, but they indicate areas of growing interest as organizations evaluate security requirements for AI workloads. Supporting different workloads across different environments The research also highlights the range of environments in which organizations deploy virtual machines. Among respondents running VMs, 64% reported using on-premises hypervisor platforms, while 51% reported using public cloud infrastructure-as-a-service (IaaS). A further 23% reported using both environments. Smaller proportions reported running VMs through KubeVirt (8%) or using MicroVM runtimes (2%). Because respondents could select multiple environments, these results reflect overlapping approaches rather than mutually exclusive deployment choices. For the cloud native ecosystem, these findings reinforce the importance of accommodating different workload characteristics and infrastructure requirements. The report also discusses technologies such as Kata Containers, which uses lightweight VMs to provide isolation for containerized workloads. Together, these approaches illustrate how virtualization and cloud native technologies can be used in different configurations depending on application and operational needs. What the findings mean for the cloud native community The findings provide a useful perspective on how production infrastructure is evolving. Virtual machines continue to account for a substantial proportion of production applications, while organizations are increasingly coordinating the teams responsible for VM and container environments. At the same time, AI and agentic workloads are introducing additional considerations around workload isolation and infrastructure utilization to drive more VM adoption. For platform engineers, infrastructure teams, developers, and security practitioners, the research highlights several areas worth exploring: how to coordinate operations across workload types, how to choose appropriate isolation boundaries, and how to manage infrastructure resources effectively. The results also underscore the value of continued collaboration across the cloud native ecosystem as organizations adopt new technologies while supporting existing applications. The future of cloud native infrastructure is not necessarily defined by a single workload or deployment model. The findings instead describe an environment in which multiple approaches continue to coexist and evolve. Explore the full research The Virtual Machines, Agentic AI and the Mix of Workloads report was authored by Adrienn Lawson of Linux Foundation Research, with a foreword by Dilpreet Bindra, Senior Director of Engineering, VCF Division, Broadcom. Sponsored by CNCF and Broadcom, the study provides data on production VM adoption, infrastructure environments, organizational coordination, AI workload isolation, and GPU utilization. We encourage the cloud native community to explore the findings...

blogs.title: Run Linux applications in hypervisor-isolated micro-VMs with Hyperlight
blogs.content: Posted on November 9, 2026 by Danilo Chiarlone, Microsoft CNCF projects highlighted in this post More and more cloud native systems run code nobody on the team wrote: the Python an AI agent generated a second ago, or a plugin a customer just uploaded. Each of them needs a boundary between that code and everything else on the host. Two recent attacks show what happens when that boundary is thin. In May 2026, the Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm ran in CI runners and on developer machines, read more than a thousand known credential locations, and hid in AI coding agents’ session hooks so it outlived even npm uninstall. In October 2026, PHP2Shell , a pair of memory-handling bugs in the PHP runtime itself, could let unauthenticated attackers run code on servers, with exploit attempts seen before the patch was out. Either the code or the runtime under it can be the thing that breaks, and what decides how much damage that does is how far the broken code can reach. The usual choices trade one property for another. A process or language sandbox starts in milliseconds, but only software stands between the code and the host: one bug in the sandbox, or in the kernel it shares with the host, and the code is out. A virtual machine puts the hypervisor in the way, but it was built to boot a whole operating system, and it takes time to start. Hyperlight , a CNCF Sandbox project, can help to close that gap. This post covers how it does it, what changed as it learned to run unmodified Linux applications (the same binaries you run on Linux today, with no porting or recompiling), and the integrations that now use it, from a Kubernetes container runtime to agent frameworks and a database. A VMM you embed Hyperlight is a library virtual machine monitor (VMM). It does not run as a separate process the way QEMU or Firecracker do: an application links it in. The core is written in Rust, with SDKs for Python and .NET. The application asks Hyperlight for a sandbox, and Hyperlight creates it as a micro-VM with its own memory, isolated by the CPU’s virtualization extensions through the host’s hypervisor: KVM or MSHV on Linux, WHP on Windows, Hypervisor.framework on macOS. A Hyperlight micro-VM carries no emulated devices and nothing else it does not need. The guest reaches the host only through the functions the host chooses to expose. What a sandbox can touch is capability-based: an allow-list the embedder writes, with no preset of permissions someone has to remember to take away. You may know Hyperlight from running WebAssembly and JavaScript through hyperlight-wasm and hyperlight-js, whose guests are built for Hyperlight. This post is about the newest member of the family, hyperlight-unikraft , which runs unmodified Linux programs. Unmodified Linux applications hyperlight-unikraft (its CLI is hluk) runs a unikernel in the micro-VM: an operating system built for one application, with one address space and only the kernel components that application needs, such as a memory allocator, a scheduler or a file system. The kernel comes from Unikraft , a Linux Foundation project. The guest runs the same binary Linux would. There is no SDK, no special libc and no recompile. Today hyperlight-unikraft runs Python, Node.js, .NET (JIT and Native AOT), Java, PHP, Go, Rust, C, Bash and PowerShell, on both x86_64 and arm64. Each runtime ships as a base rootfs, and a project can extend the base rootfs with an ordinary Dockerfile, adding packages with pip, npm or the .NET SDK. hluk build turns the result into a guest image. A Python guest that has network access can also pip install on demand. Because the guest runs ordinary Linux binaries, it can also run another sandbox, such as the Wasmtime WebAssembly runtime, and contain it when it fails. In a WasmCon 2026 talk , the Hyperlight team showed an exploit for a since-fixed Wasmtime bug ( CVE-2023-26489 ) that lets WebAssembly code read memory outside its sandbox. Run directly on the host, the exploit read secrets from the host process. Run inside hyperlight-unikraft, it could only reach the micro-VM’s own memory, and the host’s secrets stayed out of reach. The exploit and the demo are on GitHub . The hypervisor boundary turns a sandbox escape into a crashed guest. Often faster than native, with snapshots of a ready runtime Startup delays in a Python, Node.js, or .NET program are rarely caused by the operating system. They come from what the language runtime does before your code runs: importing modules, JIT-compiling, loading a framework. hyperlight-unikraft does that work once, snapshots the micro-VM at that point, and restores it in milliseconds. For a runtime with heavy startup work, a hypervisor-isolated sandbox is ready sooner than the same program started natively on the host. Each runtime image has a small driver that starts the runtime and then waits for calls from the host. When the driver is parked, the runtime is fully up and idle, and that is where hluk takes its snapshot. A project can add its own warm-up code (warm_exec = “import flask, pandas”), so the snapshot holds the libraries it uses. Later runs restore that snapshot in a few milliseconds instead of booting. The speed-up depends on how much work the runtime does up front. These are median wall times for the same script on one machine (an 8-vCPU Azure VM running KVM under nested virtualization, hluk 0.20.1, November 2026), both sides including process start ( benchmark harness on GitHub ): Workload hluk, from snapshot Native Python hello world 22 ms 17 ms Node.js hello world 39 ms 22 ms C# source compiled in the guest by Roslyn 95 ms 1,549 ms (dotnet run) Python script importing numpy, pandas, scikit-learn 45 ms 1,119 ms For a hello world the fixed costs dominate, and the micro-VM is slower. Once a runtime does real work before your code, restoring that work beats redoing it. Some runtimes have their own answers to this, such as V8 startup snapshots or Java’s CRaC. A VM snapshot is one mechanism that works the same way for every runtime, and the sandbox it restores is still isolated by the hypervisor. Because a restore is cheap, many micro-VMs can run at once from one snapshot: on the same machine, eight sharing a single Python snapshot served about 850 calls a second between them, each restoring in a few milliseconds. Where it plugs in You can use hyperlight-unikraft through the hluk CLI or embed it as a Rust library. A sandbox boots from a rootfs or a saved snapshot, with mounts and network rules declared up front: let mut sandbox = SandboxBuilder::from_snapshot_dir(cached)? .mount(Mount::ro("./data", "/mnt/data")) .network(NetworkPolicy::AllowAll) .listen_ports(ListenPorts::from_ports([8080])) .boot()?; // restores in ~3 ms sandbox.run("print(open('/mnt/data/x.csv').read())")?; Nothing is granted by default: the guest has no network and sees no host files until the embedder adds a capability for it, the way the mount and network rules above do. Integrations across the ecosystem Over the last few months, hyperlight-unikraft became the base for integrations in several ecosystems: Integration What it does urunc Runs hyperlight-unikraft guests as OCI containers under containerd, so docker run, nerdctl and Kubernetes (with a RuntimeClass) can start them, or resume them from a snapshot ( #632 , #1058 ) smolagents-hyperlight Runs a smolagents CodeAgent’s code in a micro-VM that is paused between steps mcp-server-hyperlight An MCP server whose run_python tool runs code in a micro-VM that keeps its variables between calls clickhouse-hyperlight CREATE FUNCTION … ENGINE = HyperlightPython defines a ClickHouse UDF in Python that runs in micro-VMs verl-hyperlight Runs the test cases that score a model’s code during verl training, in micro-VMs on the training node agent-sandbox Runs a Kubernetes sandbox’s Python runtime in a hyperlight-unikraft micro-VM with no RuntimeClass, so a warm pool can serve a claimed pod’s ...
